title: How Coward Teachers And Administrators Are Ruining Our Schools re-ruining-our-schools/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin opens with a detailed anecdote of a teacher who intervened to break up a physical altercation between two students, only to be undermined afterward by both a bystander colleague who refused to back her up and a supervising teacher who sided with the students' version of events. He uses the story to argue that schools collapse when administrators write policies meant to ensure safety and then decline to enforce them, and when colleagues quietly opt out of backing each other up out of self-preservation. He frames this pattern as fear-driven cowardice — fear of parents, students, media, and accusations of bias — that leads schools to abandon enforceable behavior standards altogether. His call to action is for teachers to speak up directly to administrators despite the personal risk and likely discomfort, arguing that without consistently enforced policies, discussions of curriculum and academic standards are meaningless, since the framework of enforced boundaries is what makes learning possible in the first place.
points: An anecdote about a teacher who broke up a physical altercation and was then undermined by a bystander colleague and her own supervising teacher illustrates a pattern of institutional cowardice.
Schools fail when administrators write safety and conduct policies but decline to enforce them consistently.
Colleagues who refuse to back each other up out of self-preservation compound the failure of enforcement.
The root cause is described as fear — of parents, students, media, and accusations of bias — that drives schools away from enforceable standards.
Teachers are urged to speak directly to administrators about unenforced policies despite the personal and professional risk of doing so.
quotes: One of the teachers ran toward the two students shouting “Let go, let go, let go!
The teacher was able to back away and out of physical range while calming and influencing them just enough to walk toward what was now assumed to be their supervising teacher.
The teacher who didn’t get involved, even in a back-up capacity, as well as the supervising teacher, were cowards. In the moment, when it counted, they scurried away like mice in the night.
If your school or district has cell-phone , cursing, dress-code, and conduct policies that aren’t followed as written, then you as an organization are dead.
Say something. Set up an appointment with your administrator or get yourself on the staff-meeting agenda and calmly speak your mind.
Without sensible rules, policies, and procedures enforced consistently by serious adults and a focus on skills like reading, writing, thinking, mathematics, and the arts—All hope is lost.
